content: Glyburide tablets have the potential to induce hypoglycemia. Mild hypoglycemic symptoms, which do not involve loss of consciousness or neurological abnormalities, should be managed promptly with oral glucose administration. Additionally, adjustments to the drug dosage and/or meal patterns are necessary. Continuous monitoring is essential until the physician is confident that the patient is no longer at risk. Severe hypoglycemic reactions, which may involve coma, seizures, or other neurological impairments, are rare but represent medical emergencies that require immediate hospitalization. If hypoglycemic coma is diagnosed or suspected, the patient should receive a rapid intravenous injection of a concentrated (50%) glucose solution. This should be followed by a continuous infusion of a more diluted (10%) glucose solution at a rate sufficient to maintain blood glucose levels above 100 mg/dL. Patients must be closely monitored for at least 24 to 48 hours, as hypoglycemia can recur even after apparent clinical recovery. Pharmacology Mechanism of Action Glyburide acutely lowers blood glucose levels by stimulating insulin release from the pancreas. This effect is dependent on the presence of functioning beta cells in the pancreatic islets. The mechanism by which glyburide maintains blood glucose reduction during long-term administration is not fully understood. In patients with Type II diabetes, the glucose-lowering effect persists with chronic use, even as the insulin secretory response to the drug diminishes over time. It is possible that extrapancreatic effects contribute to the action of oral sulfonylurea hypoglycemic drugs. The combination of glyburide and metformin may produce a synergistic effect, as both agents improve glucose tolerance through different but complementary mechanisms. Some patients who initially respond to oral hypoglycemic drugs, including glyburide, may become unresponsive or poorly responsive over time. Conversely, glyburide may be effective in certain patients who have become unresponsive to one or more other sulfonylurea drugs. In addition to its glucose-lowering effects, glyburide induces mild diuresis by enhancing renal free water clearance. Disulfiram-like reactions have been very rarely reported in patients treated with glyburide tablets. Structure Glyburide tablets USP contain glyburide, USP, an oral blood-glucose-lowering drug of the sulfonylurea class. Glyburide, USP, is a white crystalline compound. Its chemical name is 1-((p-(2-(5-chloro-o-anisamido)ethyl)phenyl)sulfonyl)-3-cyclohexylurea. Each tablet contains either 1.25 mg, 2.5 mg, or 5 mg of glyburide, USP. In addition, the tablets include the following inactive ingredients: microcrystalline cellulose, pregelatinized corn starch, sodium starch glycolate, colloidal silicon dioxide, and magnesium stearate. The 5 mg tablets contain FD&C Yellow No. 6 aluminum lake, D&C Yellow No. 10 aluminum lake, and FD&C Blue No. 1 aluminum lake. Pharmacodynamics There is limited information available regarding the pharmacodynamics of glyburide in the drug label. Pharmacokinetics Single-dose studies in healthy subjects demonstrate significant absorption of glyburide within one hour, with peak drug levels occurring approximately four hours after administration. Low but detectable levels of the drug are present at 24 hours. Mean serum levels of glyburide, as reflected by the area under the serum concentration-time curve, increase proportionally with corresponding increases in dose. Multiple-dose studies in diabetic patients show that the drug concentration-time curves are similar to those observed in single-dose studies, indicating no accumulation of the drug in tissue depots. The decline of glyburide in the serum of healthy individuals follows a biphasic pattern, with a terminal half-life of approximately 10 hours. In single-dose studies conducted in fasting healthy subjects, the degree and duration of blood glucose reduction are proportional to the administered dose and the area under the drug concentration-time curve. The glucose-lowering effect persists for 24 hours following a single morning dose in non-fasting diabetic patients. However, under conditions of repeated administration in diabetic patients, there is no reliable correlation between blood drug levels and fasting blood glucose levels. A one-year study in diabetic patients treated with glyburide showed no consistent correlation between the administered dose and serum drug levels. The major metabolite of glyburide is the 4-trans-hydroxy derivative, with a secondary metabolite being the 3-cis-hydroxy derivative. These metabolites likely contribute minimally to hypoglycemic action in humans, as they are only weakly active (1/400th and 1/40th as active, respectively, as glyburide) in rabbits. Glyburide is excreted as metabolites in both bile and urine, with approximately 50% eliminated via each route.
